column1: # Absolute home paths that a tracked file may legitimately contain (backlog-216).
# Format: <citing/file>::<home-root><TAB><reason>
# The token is the HOME ROOT -- the first two path components plus the trailing
# slash, e.g. the container account a Dockerfile builds under -- not a whole
# path. One row therefore covers every line in that file that reaches into the
# same home, which is how these actually cluster (the Dockerfile has twelve).
# Rows are SCOPED ONLY: there is no bare form. Every legitimate case found by
# the backlog-216 sweep was legitimate BECAUSE of the file it was in -- an image
# build, a CI comment about a container, a gate documenting its own regex, a
# captured tool log. None of them is a reason to wave the same home root through
# a design document. A bare row would do exactly that, so the parser refuses one.
# A row without a TAB and a reason is exit 2, not a pass: an exemption whose
# justification is missing is indistinguishable from a paste.
# This file is itself scanned. A home path here is skipped only when it is the
# first field of a well-formed row; one in a comment, or in a row missing its
# reason, is a finding like any other. That is deliberate -- the file whose job
# is to list these paths is the easiest place for a real one to hide.
Dockerfile::/home/opam/
column2: the opam base image's own account; the path is fixed by the IMAGE, not by whoever runs the build, and OPAMROOT/WORKDIR must name it absolutely

column1: .github/workflows/ci.yml::/home/rocq/
column2: prose in a comment explaining why a `container:` job fails: the rocq image's switch belongs to its own `rocq` user, which is the fact being recorded
